claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal alloys in a single-phase solid-solution state.
Annealing at 0.5 to 0.8 Tm is sufficient to activate atomic diffusion while remaining below the melting point.
For nanoparticles below 10 nm, the surface-to-volume ratio is sufficiently significant to affect structural evolution.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered solid solution.
Elevated-temperature structural evolution is governed by competition between configurational-entropy stabilization and surface-energy-driven segregation.
The constituent element with the lowest surface energy preferentially migrates to the nanoparticle surface.
Preferential surface migration of the lowest-surface-energy element produces a core-shell structure.
At the nanoscale, the total free energy is dominated by the surface contribution γA.
Surface segregation lowers the total surface free energy.
Surface-energy minimization can override bulk configurational-entropy stabilization in sufficiently small nanoparticles.
Surface segregation can destabilize the initial single-phase solid solution.
Limited diffusion kinetics may cause phase separation or amorphization.
Nanoparticles may undergo phase separation or secondary-phase crystallization at lower temperatures than bulk thermodynamic models predict.
Traditional alloying concepts and bulk HENA models use ΔS_config ≥ 1.5 R as a criterion for intrinsic single-phase solid-solution stability.
Bulk HENA models predict stability against phase separation up to the melting point when surface effects are neglected.
The intrinsic-stability model fails below approximately 10 nm when surface-energy contributions exceed configurational-entropy stabilization.
A large difference among the constituent elements' surface energies promotes failure of the intrinsic-stability model.
